title: Chromatic Aberration of Lenses
short_intro: Chromatic aberration is an optical defect in lenses caused by the dependence of refractive index on the wavelength of light, leading to dispersion of white light into constituent colors at different focal points. It prevents a single-element lens from forming a sharp, single-point white-light image.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition, cause of chromatic aberration, longitudinal and lateral chromatic aberration, focal length variation for different colors, and condition for achromatism of two thin lenses in contact.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Achromatic combination of two thin lenses separated by a finite distance, dispersive power, achromatism for lenses separated by a distance, and evaluation of radii of curvature for minimizing aberration.

prerequisites: Snell's Law and Refraction through spherical surfaces
Lens Maker's Formula and thin lens optics
Dispersive power of optical materials and Cauchy's dispersion formula

concept_notes.heading: Origin of Chromatic Aberration
bullets: The refractive index (μ) of lens material varies inversely with wavelength (λ) according to Cauchy's relation: μ = A + B/λ².
Violet light (λ is short) experiences a higher refractive index than red light (λ is long), resulting in μ<sub>v</sub> > μ<sub>r</sub>.
From the Lens Maker's Formula, focal length f is given by 1/f = (μ - 1)(1/R<sub>1</sub> - 1/R<sub>2</sub>), causing violet light to focus closer to the lens than red light.

concept_notes.heading: Longitudinal and Lateral Chromatic Aberration
bullets: Longitudinal Chromatic Aberration (LCA) is the axial separation between the focal points of extreme colors (violet and red): LCA = f<sub>r</sub> - f<sub>v</sub>.
Lateral Chromatic Aberration (TCA) is the difference in image sizes for different wavelengths formed in a plane perpendicular to the optical axis.
For an axial object, LCA manifests as a blurred colored patch along the optic axis, whereas TCA causes colored fringes around off-axis image points.

concept_notes.heading: Dispersive Power of Lens Material
bullets: Dispersive power (ω) is defined as the ratio of the difference in focal lengths (or refractive indices) for extreme colors to the focal length (or refractive index) for the mean color.
ω = (f<sub>r</sub> - f<sub>v</sub>)/f<sub>y</sub> = (μ<sub>v</sub> - μ<sub>r</sub>)/(μ<sub>y</sub> - 1), where subscripts v, r, and y denote violet, red, and yellow (mean) rays.
Dispersive power is a dimensionless quantity characteristic of the optical medium, typically glass.

concept_notes.heading: Achromatic Combination of Lenses
bullets: Achromatism aims to bring rays of extreme wavelengths (e.g., red and violet) to a common focus, eliminating chromatic aberration.

Two thin lenses of dispersive powers ω<sub>1</sub> and ω<sub>2</sub> and focal lengths f<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>2</sub> achieve achromatism when ω<sub>1</sub>/f<sub>1</sub> + ω<sub>2</sub>/f<sub>2</sub> = 0.
To achieve a real, positive focal length for the combination, one lens must be convex (crown glass) and the other concave (flint glass), requiring ω<sub>1</sub> ≠ ω<sub>2</sub>.

derivations.title: Condition for Achromatism of Two Thin Lenses in Contact
derivations.conditions: Two thin lenses placed coaxially in contact, illuminated by white light.
steps: Write the equivalent focal length F of two thin lenses in contact: 1/F = 1/f<sub>1</sub> + 1/f<sub>2</sub>.
Differentiate the equation with respect to wavelength to find the change in focal power: d(1/F) = d(1/f<sub>1</sub>) + d(1/f<sub>2</sub>).
Using the definition of dispersive power ω = -df/f, substitute df/f<sup>2</sup> = -ω/f into the differentiated expression.
Set d(1/F) = 0 for chromatic aberration to vanish: ω<sub>1</sub>/f<sub>1</sub> + ω<sub>2</sub>/f<sub>2</sub> = 0.

derivations.title: Condition for Achromatism of Two Thin Lenses Separated by a Distance
derivations.conditions: Two thin lenses of focal lengths f<sub>1</sub> and f<sub>2</sub> separated by a finite distance d.
steps: Write the equivalent focal length F for two lenses separated by distance d: 1/F = 1/f<sub>1</sub> + 1/f<sub>2</sub> - d/(f<sub>1</sub>f<sub>2</sub>).
Differentiate implicitly with respect to wavelength, noting dispersive powers ω<sub>1</sub> = -df<sub>1</sub>/f<sub>1</sub> and ω<sub>2</sub> = -df<sub>2</sub>/f<sub>2</sub>.
Apply the condition for achromatism by equating the derivative of the reciprocal focal length with respect to wavelength to zero.
Simplify the resulting algebraic expression to obtain the separation d in terms of focal lengths and dispersive powers.

formula_sheet.name: Cauchy Dispersion Formula
formula_sheet.variables: A, B are material constants, λ is wavelength
formula_sheet.conditions: Valid in spectral regions away from absorption bands

formula_sheet.name: Lens Maker's Formula
formula_sheet.variables: f is focal length, μ is refractive index, R<sub>1</sub>, R<sub>2</sub> are radii of curvature

formula_sheet.name: Dispersive Power
formula_sheet.variables: μ<sub>v</sub>, μ<sub>r</sub>, μ<sub>y</sub> are refractive indices for violet, red, yellow rays

formula_sheet.name: Longitudinal Chromatic Aberration (LCA)
formula_sheet.variables: f<sub>r</sub>, f<sub>v</sub> are focal lengths for red and violet light, ω is dispersive power

formula_sheet.name: Equivalent Focal Length of Two Lenses in Contact
formula_sheet.variables: F is equivalent focal length, f<sub>1</sub>, f<sub>2</sub> are individual focal lengths

formula_sheet.name: Achromatic Condition (Contact Lenses)
formula_sheet.variables: ω<sub>1</sub>, ω<sub>2</sub> are dispersive powers, f<sub>1</sub>, f<sub>2</sub> are focal lengths
formula_sheet.conditions: Minimum chromatic aberration for white light

formula_sheet.name: Equivalent Focal Length for Separated Lenses
formula_sheet.variables: d is separation distance between the two lenses
formula_sheet.conditions: Coaxial thin lenses separated by distance d

formula_sheet.name: Achromatic Condition (Separated Lenses)
formula_sheet.equation_html: d = \frac{f_1 f_2 (\omega_1 + \omega_2)}{\omega_1 f_2 + \omega_2 f_1} \text{ (general)} \implies d = \frac{f_1 + f_2}{2} \text{ (same material)}
formula_sheet.variables: d is separation, f<sub>1</sub>, f<sub>2</sub> focal lengths, ω<sub>1</sub>, ω<sub>2</sub> dispersive powers
formula_sheet.conditions: Coaxial system of two lenses of the same material

graphs_and_experiments.title: Focal Length vs Wavelength Plot
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve showing focal length (f) on the y-axis against wavelength (λ) on the x-axis, exhibiting an upward monotonic increase from violet to red.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that shorter wavelengths focus closer to the optical center than longer wavelengths due to dispersion.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Interpreting focal shift and identifying positions of chromatic aberration extremes.

graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: White light incident on a crown-flint glass doublet, showing parallel white rays refracting through both lenses and converging to a single white focal point.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates how combining lenses with compensating dispersive powers corrects longitudinal chromatic aberration.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tracing refracted paths of red and violet components in compound lens systems.

solved_numericals.question: A thin convex lens made of glass has a focal length of 0.30 m for yellow light. If the dispersive power of the glass is 0.02, calculate the longitudinal chromatic aberration between red and violet light.
solution_steps: Identify given values: mean focal length f<sub>y</sub> = 0.30 m, dispersive power ω = 0.02.
Use the formula for longitudinal chromatic aberration: LCA = ω × f<sub>y</sub>.

solved_numericals.question: An achromatic doublet is formed by two lenses in contact. The focal length of the combination for yellow light is 0.40 m. If the dispersive powers of the two glass materials are 0.03 and 0.05, find the individual focal lengths of the two lenses.
solution_steps: Given: Equivalent focal length F = 0.40 m, ω<sub>1</sub> = 0.03, ω<sub>2</sub> = 0.05.

Condition for achromatism in contact: ω<sub>1</sub>/f<sub>1</sub> + ω<sub>2</sub>/f<sub>2</sub> = 0, which gives f<sub>2</sub> = -(ω<sub>2</sub>/ω<sub>1</sub>)f<sub>1</sub> = -(0.05/0.03)f<sub>1</sub> = -(5/3)f<sub>1</sub>.
Use the combination formula for contact lenses: 1/F = 1/f<sub>1</sub> + 1/f<sub>2</sub> = 1/f<sub>1</sub> - (3/5)/f<sub>1</sub> = (2/5)/f<sub>1</sub>.
Solve for f<sub>1</sub>: f<sub>1</sub> = (2/5) × F = (2/5) × 0.40 = 0.16 m.

solved_numericals.question: Two thin lenses of the same material are separated by a distance d to form an achromatic system. If the focal length of each lens is 0.20 m, calculate the separation d.
solution_steps: For two lenses of the same material (ω<sub>1</sub> = ω<sub>2</sub>) separated by distance d, the condition for achromatism is d = (f<sub>1</sub> + f<sub>2</sub>)/2.

assumptions_and_limitations: The thin lens approximation is assumed, neglecting lens thickness in optical center calculations.
Paraxial ray approximation is used; chromatic aberration formulas do not account for off-axis monochromatic aberrations like coma or astigmatism unless coupled.
Cauchy's dispersion formula is an empirical approximation valid only across visible wavelengths.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Chromatic aberration can be completely eliminated for all wavelengths using a two-lens achromatic doublet.
common_misconceptions.correct: An achromatic doublet brings only two extreme wavelengths (usually red and F-blue/violet) to a common focus.
common_misconceptions.why: A secondary spectrum remains because the ratio of dispersive powers is not constant across the entire spectrum.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Concave lenses do not exhibit chromatic aberration.
common_misconceptions.correct: All refractive optical elements made of dispersive media exhibit chromatic aberration, regardless of whether they are converging or diverging.
common_misconceptions.why: Dispersion is an inherent property of refraction through any material where μ varies with λ.

quick_revision: Chromatic aberration arises due to the wavelength dependence of refractive index (μ ∝ 1/λ²).
